summary: An experimental change to TCP congestion control that makes it back off less than usual when it receives an ECN signal. This improves performance on bottlenecks using short queues from AQM.

eli5.summary: When told gently that the road is getting full, you slow down a little instead of a lot.

subtitle: Softer backoff when the network gently signals congestion, improving throughput on modern AQM buffers.

tldr.problem: Modern routers use Active Queue Management (AQM) to keep queues short and reduce latency, but TCP reacts to their early congestion signals the same way it reacts to packet loss, causing it to back off too aggressively and underuse the link.
tldr.mechanism: TCP Alternative Backoff with ECN (ABE) changes TCP to reduce its congestion window by 20% (multiply by 0.8) when it sees an Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) mark, instead of the usual 50% reduction it applies to actual packet loss.
tldr.outcome: The protocol is experimental. Tests showed better throughput on bottlenecks with AQM without losing the latency benefits those systems provide.

today: RFC 8511 is Experimental. It has been implemented on Linux and merged into FreeBSD mainline. Deployment in production systems is ongoing, and standardization as a proposed standard is planned once the experiment yields results.

sections.title: The Problem: AQM, Congestion, and TCP
sections.content:
TCP's congestion control has worked well for decades, but modern routers are changing how they handle congestion. Instead of letting queues grow until packets are dropped, Active Queue Management (AQM) systems like CoDel and PIE mark packets with an Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) flag early, while there is still buffer space. This lets more packets reach their destination than would if the router had dropped them.

However, TCP currently treats an ECN mark the same as a dropped packet: it cuts its congestion window in half. This aggressive response makes sense when the network is truly exhausted (packet loss), but is overkill for the early warning that an AQM system sends. The result is that TCP backs off too much, fails to use the available bandwidth, and suffers latency problems on paths with a large bandwidth-delay product (BDP) despite the AQM system trying to keep latency low.
sections.eli5: Imagine you are driving on a road where the lights turn yellow to warn of traffic ahead. If you slam on the brakes like you would in a crash, you will waste the road's capacity and frustrate cars behind you. An early warning deserves a gentler response.

sections.title: How ABE Works: Different Responses to Different Signals
sections.content:
ABE decouples TCP's response to the two types of congestion feedback: inferred packet loss and ECN signals. When TCP detects that a packet was lost, it still uses the traditional aggressive backoff, multiplying the congestion window by 0.5. When TCP receives an ECN-Echo flag indicating an ECN mark from the network, ABE instead multiplies by 0.8, cutting the window by only 20% instead of 50%.

More formally, ABE introduces two separate parameters: beta_loss (the traditional 0.5 for loss-detected congestion) and beta_ecn (0.8 for ECN-marked congestion). The RFC specifies that beta_ecn should be 0.8 for standard TCP Reno; other algorithms like CUBIC may use different values (e.g., 0.85).
sections.eli5: TCP now has two reaction modes: a panic mode for actual crashes (multiply by 0.5) and a caution mode for yellow lights (multiply by 0.8).

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment
sections.content:
ABE is a sender-side-only change. The TCP receiver does not need to know about it, and network routers do not need to change. Only the sending TCP stack needs to be modified to recognize ECN-Echo flags and apply the 0.8 multiplier instead of 0.5. This makes deployment straightforward: implementations can enable ABE without requiring coordination across the network.

The RFC notes that ABE is safe to deploy incrementally. If only some senders use ABE while others do not, ABE senders gain an advantage on ECN-marked congestion. If any ABE sender becomes too aggressive despite the reduced backoff, the AQM mechanism will still drop packets, and at that point TCP will use the aggressive 0.5 backoff, falling back to traditional behavior.
sections.eli5: Only your car needs to be smart about yellow lights. Other cars, the traffic lights, and the road itself do not need changes.

sections.title: Why This Matters: AQM and Shallow Queues
sections.content:
The RFC anchors ABE to research on the mismatch between traditional TCP and modern AQM. CoDel and PIE are designed to keep sustained queue length short, which reduces latency for interactive applications. However, a TCP sender with a large BDP (e.g., a long-distance, high-bandwidth link) needs to have many segments in flight to fill the pipe. When it receives an ECN mark and cuts its window by 50%, it suddenly has far fewer segments in flight, leading to a gap in transmission and link underutilization.

AQM systems only mark packets when the queue exceeds a delay threshold, not when the buffer is full. An ECN mark therefore signals 'your traffic is using too much buffer delay' rather than 'we are dropping packets because we have no buffer space'. ABE's softer response respects this distinction, maintaining throughput while still reducing queue depth.
sections.eli5: A yellow light means 'the road is getting busy', not 'the road is completely full'. You should slow down, but not to a crawl.

sections.title: Experiment and Future Direction
sections.content:
This RFC is Experimental. The authors expect it will be proposed as a Standards-Track document in the future once the IETF gains experience with deployments. The main questions for the experiment are: does ABE work safely and effectively in real networks, and do AQM and TCP implementations converge on this approach?

ABE has been implemented as patches for Linux and FreeBSD and tested with NewReno and CUBIC algorithms over CoDel and PIE. The FreeBSD patch was merged into the mainline kernel in March 2018.
sections.eli5: This is a test of a new idea. If it works well in practice, it may become part of the official TCP standard.
